prompt: Where does the code inside a Lambda function get its AWS credentials from?
hint: Lambda assumes something for the function and hands over the result.

choices.text: From the execution role, as temporary credentials in its environment
choices.why: Right. Lambda assumes the role and puts the session into AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_SESSION_TOKEN.

choices.text: From the account's root user
choices.why: Nothing in a function runs as root; it runs as its role.

choices.text: From the user who deployed the function, whose permissions it keeps
choices.why: The deployer's permissions end with the deployment. The function runs as the role named in its configuration.

choices.text: From an access key the developer pastes into the handler
choices.why: A function needs no key of its own, and a key in the code is lesson 7's problem.

prompt: After caio attached `AdministratorAccess` to the export function's role, what could a flaw in one of the function's libraries reach?
hint: The role's session read a patient file in the lab.

choices.text: Just `clinic-exports`, the bucket the function writes to
choices.why: That is what the function does, not what its role allows. The session read `clinic-records` too.

choices.text: Every resource the account holds
choices.why: Right. Any code in the function inherits the role, and that role refused nothing.

choices.text: The function's own copy and no further, since Lambda isolates each copy
choices.why: Lambda isolates copies from each other, not the role's credentials from the account.

choices.text: What the function's handler names in its code
choices.why: The role does not read the code. A library can call any API the role allows.

prompt: Which piece of evidence does the lesson treat as the proof that the narrow policy works?
hint: A policy is what you meant.

choices.text: The old session, whose permissions change at once
choices.why: The lesson asks for a new session, so the proof does not depend on how a session already issued behaves.

choices.text: The `write-exports.json` file, read carefully
choices.why: The file says what was meant; only a request shows what the account does.

choices.text: `put-role-policy` returning without an error
choices.why: That proves the policy was stored, not what it allows.

choices.text: A new session that still writes the export and is refused the patient file and the user list
choices.why: Right. The work still works, and what it had no business doing is refused.

prompt: After testing, ana leaves her `admin` user in the export role's trust policy "in case it is useful". What has she left open?
hint: The trust policy answers who may become the role.

choices.text: A way for the function to act as admin
choices.why: Trust runs the other way: it lets admin act as the function's role, not the function as admin.

choices.text: Public access to the function's URL
choices.why: Who may call the function is a different document, its resource-based policy.

choices.text: No risk, because admin already holds AdministratorAccess
choices.why: Today. A trust entry outlives the reason for it: whoever later holds admin's key, or a narrowed admin, still becomes the role.

choices.text: A second way into the function's permissions
choices.why: Right. Only the Lambda service should become an execution role.

prompt: Which of these are ways the lesson names to find out what actions a function really needs? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three ways, all from AWS's documentation.

choices.text: The role's last accessed information
choices.why: Right. It lists the services the role used and when.

choices.text: Sharing one role across the functions so each finds what it needs
choices.why: A shared role carries the union of every function's needs.

choices.text: Reading the code, where each SDK call is an action
choices.why: Right. `put_object` is `s3:PutObject`.

choices.text: IAM Access Analyzer drafting a policy from CloudTrail activity
choices.why: Right. It keeps only the actions it saw used.

choices.text: Attaching AdministratorAccess until the errors stop
choices.why: That is caio's mistake: the errors stop because every limit stops.

prompt: A function URL has `AuthType` `NONE` and a resource-based policy allowing `"*"` to invoke it. Who can start the function?
hint: No signature is required.

choices.text: Users of the clinic's account who know the URL
choices.why: Nothing about the request has to come from the account: it needs no signature at all.

choices.text: Anybody on the internet
choices.why: Right. The principal is everybody and no signature is required.

choices.text: Nobody, until the function is published to API Gateway
choices.why: A function URL is its own HTTPS endpoint, with no gateway in front.

choices.text: The reception's tablet, since that is what it was made for
choices.why: Intent is not a control. Nothing in either setting names the tablet.

prompt: Why does the lesson say an address that is hard to guess is not an access control?
hint: Think of where an address ends up.

choices.text: Because moto prints it in its terminal
choices.why: That is the lab, not the reason.

choices.text: Because function URLs are listed publicly by AWS
choices.why: AWS publishes no list. The address leaks through ordinary places.

choices.text: Because an address that answers ends up in logs, histories, screenshots and scanners
choices.why: Right. Secrecy of the address is not a decision about who may call it.

choices.text: Because the random part of the address is short enough for a scanner to try each value in an afternoon
choices.why: The random part is long; it leaks rather than being guessed.

prompt: After `remove-permission`, `aws lambda get-policy` answered `ResourceNotFoundException`. What does that tell you?
hint: What resource was not found?

choices.text: moto lost track of the function after the URL changed type
choices.why: It is the documented answer for a function with no policy, and AWS gives the same one.

choices.text: The URL still allows anybody; just the statement id changed
choices.why: The statement is gone and the URL now demands a signature.

choices.text: The function was deleted along with the permission
choices.why: The function is still there; its URL was updated a line earlier.

choices.text: The function has no resource-based policy at all
choices.why: Right. Nobody outside the account is allowed to call it.

prompt: A permission lets `s3.amazonaws.com` invoke a function, with no condition. Which bucket can make it run?
hint: The service name covers more than your account.

choices.text: Any bucket in any account, set up to notify the function
choices.why: Right. That is the confused deputy, and the source ARN and account close it.

choices.text: No bucket, until the bucket's owner writes a bucket policy that names the function
choices.why: The bucket's notification is configured on the bucket, by its owner; the function's permission is what is checked.

choices.text: `clinic-uploads`, the bucket caio meant
choices.why: Only once the statement says so, with `--source-arn`.

choices.text: Buckets in the function's own account
choices.why: Nothing in the statement says so. That is what `--source-account` adds.

prompt: Why does the S3 permission name the account as well as the bucket?
hint: A bucket name is not owned for ever.

choices.text: Because AWS rejects a source ARN without an account
choices.why: AWS accepts it; the lesson names the account for a reason of its own.

choices.text: A bucket ARN names no account, and a deleted bucket's name is free for another account to take
choices.why: Right. The account ties the name to its owner.

choices.text: Because moto ignores the bucket and only judges the account
choices.why: moto judges neither; it ignores conditions.

choices.text: To make the function cheaper to call
choices.why: Conditions change who may call, not the price.

prompt: Lambda encrypts environment variables at rest. Why is a password there still exposed?
hint: Who gets the decrypted value?

choices.text: Lambda stores a second copy unencrypted for debugging
choices.why: No such copy is needed; the API returns the value decrypted.

choices.text: The encryption uses a weak algorithm
choices.why: The algorithm is not the issue; who it is decrypted for is.

choices.text: Because it is decrypted for every caller allowed to read the configuration
choices.why: Right. Encryption at rest says nothing about who reads it through the API.

choices.text: The key is printed in the function's logs
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson prints a key; the value comes back from a read of the configuration.

prompt: bia has only `ReadOnlyAccess`. Which of these could she do with the clinic's function as the lesson first found it?
hint: Look at the actions the policy grants for Lambda.

choices.text: Read the database password from the function's configuration
choices.why: Right. `lambda:Get*` covers `GetFunctionConfiguration`.

choices.text: Invoke the function and receive the password in the answer
choices.why: Invoking is not reading; she does not need to, the configuration already holds the value.

choices.text: Change the database password in the function
choices.why: Read-only grants no update action.

choices.text: No harm, since read-only users see names and not configuration
choices.why: `lambda:Get*` is configuration reading, and the policy grants it.

prompt: After the fix, what does the function's environment hold?
hint: The handler reads one variable and asks for the rest.

choices.text: The name of the secret, `clinic/db`
choices.why: Right. A name harms nobody; the value is fetched at run time by the role.

choices.text: No variables: the password is compiled into the zip
choices.why: A secret in the package is the same exposure in a different file, and it is lesson 12's subject.

choices.text: The ARN of the execution role
choices.why: The role is in the function's configuration, not in its environment variables.

choices.text: The password, encrypted with a key of the clinic's own
choices.why: A customer key changes who can decrypt at rest, but the value would still be in the configuration.

prompt: `ReadOnlyAccess` lets bia list secrets but not call `secretsmanager:___`, so she cannot read what they hold.
hint: The action the execution role was given on one secret.

prompt: The password has been moved from the environment into Secrets Manager. What else does the lesson say must happen?
hint: The secret has a past.

choices.text: Remove ReadOnlyAccess from the analysts
choices.why: The policy is fine for what it is; the value should never have been in a field it reads.

choices.text: No further step; moving it closes the exposure
choices.why: It closes it from now on. Everybody who could read it before may still hold it.

choices.text: Delete the function and create it again so the old configuration is forgotten
choices.why: The old value is already out in whoever read it; recreating the function does not reach them.

choices.text: Change the password in the database too
choices.why: Right. It was readable by every read-only user for as long as it sat there.

prompt: Lambda keeps the Python runtime patched. Who patches the libraries inside the function's zip file?
hint: They were frozen the day it was built.

choices.text: pip, automatically, each time a copy starts
choices.why: Nothing installs anything when a copy starts; it runs the package as built.

choices.text: The library's authors, who push fixes to the functions using it
choices.why: They publish new versions; your package does not change until you rebuild it.

choices.text: Lambda, along with the runtime
choices.why: The runtime is the interpreter and the system; the zip is yours.

choices.text: You, and nobody else, by rebuilding and redeploying
choices.why: Right. Nobody patches it but you.

prompt: `pip-audit` reported 10 known vulnerabilities for `requests==2.19.1` on the day the lesson was recorded. Why might the same command report more next month?
hint: What changes, if the version does not?

choices.text: New advisories get published about the old version
choices.why: Right. The version stays, the knowledge about it grows, so the scan is repeated.

choices.text: requirements.txt resolves to a different version each month
choices.why: It pins `==2.19.1`; that does not move.

choices.text: Lambda reports its runtime's flaws into the audit
choices.why: pip-audit reads the list of packages, not Lambda.

choices.text: pip-audit's own version changes on its own
choices.why: It is pinned at 2.10.1 and does not upgrade itself.

prompt: caio fixes the pin in `requirements.txt`, the audit comes back clean, and he stops there. What is still wrong?
hint: The audit read a file; the function runs a zip.

choices.text: The audit should have been run twice
choices.why: A second clean audit of the same file adds nothing.

choices.text: The function still runs the old package until it is rebuilt and deployed
choices.why: Right. A fixed file beside an old package fixes nothing.

choices.text: He should have removed `requests` altogether
choices.why: The function uses it; the fix is a newer version, which he chose.

choices.text: pip-audit checks direct dependencies and skips indirect ones
choices.why: With `--no-deps` it checks the file as written; without it, it resolves what they pull in. Neither is what is left undone here.

prompt: Which of these habits does the lesson recommend for what goes into a function's package? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three habits.

choices.text: Package only what the handler imports
choices.why: Right. An unimported library is one less row in every audit.

choices.text: Copy the developer's whole virtual environment, so nothing is missing
choices.why: That ships test tools and notebooks too.

choices.text: Audit layers as you audit the function
choices.why: Right. A layer is a dependency shared between functions.

choices.text: Rebuild on a schedule as well as on a change
choices.why: Right. The untouched function carries a year of advisories.

choices.text: Leave versions unpinned so the newest gets installed
choices.why: Unpinned versions make the audit say nothing about what runs.

prompt: Match each edge of a function to the document that decides it.
hint: The figure at the start of the lesson.

prompt: Put the steps of moving a password out of a function's environment in order.
hint: Last comes the part about the past.
items: store the password in Secrets Manager
put the secret's name in the environment instead of the value
allow the execution role to read that one secret
deploy a handler that fetches the value at run time
change the password in the database
trap: Changing the password first is the slip: the function would break until the new value is stored where it reads it.

prompt: A function URL whose authentication type is `___` demands that every request be signed.
hint: The value the fix moved it to.

prompt: How many actions did the narrow `write-exports` policy allow?
hint: One action on one place.

prompt: Ten small functions share one execution role that allows the union of what they need. One of them has a flaw. What does the flaw reach?
hint: A role does not know which function is using it.

choices.text: No more than before, because a shared role is read-only
choices.why: Sharing changes nothing about what a role may do.

choices.text: The other nine functions' code, not their data
choices.why: The role reaches whatever its policies allow, data included.

choices.text: What that one function needs
choices.why: The role allows the union, and the flaw holds the role.

choices.text: Every permission any of the ten needs
choices.why: Right. One function, one role.
